title: The Transistor
objective: After this level you can explain how the 1947 transistor replaced hot, fragile vacuum tubes as the computer's switch.
summary: Vacuum tubes switched with heated cathodes that used power and burned out. In 1947 Bardeen and Brattain made the transistor at Bell Labs: a small, cool, reliable switch that replaced tubes.

cards.headline: ENIAC lost one of its vacuum tubes roughly every day or two.
cards.body: It had about 18,000 of them, and each one was a switch that could fail. Computing needed a switch that didn't run hot and burn out.

cards.headline: A switch that's also a heater
cards.body: A vacuum tube controls a stream of electrons. To get those electrons, its cathode is heated to about 1,000°C or more, which takes significant power and gives off a lot of heat. And like an old light bulb, tubes tend to burn out, mainly when their heated filaments fail.

cards.headline: Three physicists at Bell Labs
cards.body: In December 1947 at Bell Labs, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain made the first working transistor, from a small piece of germanium. They worked in a solid-state physics group organized by William Shockley. In 1956 the three shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for their discovery of the transistor effect. A team effort, not a lone genius.

cards.fact: Transistors are small, run cool, are highly reliable and use little power.
cards.context: A transistor can work as a switch: if current flows, the circuit is on, and if not, it's off. That's the on-off switch that stores Level 2's bits. By the late 1950s transistors had replaced vacuum tubes in many uses, and complex circuits could shrink.

questions.prompt: Why did vacuum tubes use so much power and give off so much heat?

options.label: They were made of germanium, which runs hot
options.rationale: Germanium was used in the first transistor.

options.label: Their cathodes had to be heated to release electrons
They were cooled with water that needed pumping
options.rationale: Cooling isn't what used their power.

options.label: They stored the whole program inside the glass
options.rationale: Tubes were switches, not program stores.

questions.explanation: A tube's cathode is heated to about 1,000°C or more to give off electrons, which takes significant power.

questions.prompt: Level 2 said a transistor switch stores a bit. How does a transistor act as that switch?

options.label: It glows brightly whenever it's switched on
options.rationale: That's closer to a vacuum tube.

options.label: A tiny lever inside it flips up or down
options.rationale: Transistors have no moving parts to flip.

options.label: It spins faster to show a 1 than a 0
options.rationale: It works by current, not motion.

options.label: Current flowing means on; no current means off

questions.explanation: If current flows, the circuit is on (1); if not, it's off (0).
